hints: Start by thinking about where the blood is at all times. Does it stay inside tubes or does it spill out to bathe the cells directly?
Now trace one red blood cell on a full journey - from the heart to the lungs, back to the heart, then to the body and back to the heart. How many times does it pass through the heart?
walkthrough:
Why Closed Means Staying Inside Pipes**
Think of the blood system like central heating pipes that never leak. In mammals blood never leaves the vessels to slosh around the tissues. It flows from heart to arteries to capillaries to veins and back to the heart. That confinement is what closed means.

Why Double Means Twice Through the Heart**
Now follow the loop. The right side of the heart pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs - that is the pulmonary circuit. Oxygenated blood returns to the left side, which then pumps it to the rest of the body - that is the systemic circuit. So in one full tour of the body, blood enters the heart twice.

Final answer: closed - blood is always contained within blood vessels (heart, arteries, veins, capillaries); double - blood passes through the heart twice for one complete circulation of the body, in pulmonary and systemic circuits.

hints: Section A-B is a cut high up through the top of the heart, viewed from above. Focus on what enters the top chambers and what valves sit at the base of the big outgoing arteries.
Remember left and right are reversed when you look at a front view, and think about which thin-walled vessel brings oxygenated blood back from the lungs on the left side.
Look for the small circular valve with three cusps in the centre, and the thin-walled receiving chamber on the opposite side to the pulmonary vein.
walkthrough:
Reading a Top Slice From Above**
Fig. 5.2 is high up, so you see atria and the roots of the aorta and pulmonary artery, not the thick ventricles. Structure 1 is a thin-walled vessel joining the large chamber on the B side. That side is the left atrium, and the only vessels entering it are the pulmonary veins bringing oxygenated blood from the lungs.

Spotting Valves and the Other Atrium**
Structure 2 shows the classic three half-moon cusps seen in cross-section. Those are semilunar valves, here the pulmonary valve at the base of the pulmonary artery, which prevent backflow into the ventricle. Structure 3 is the smaller, thin-walled chamber on the A side. That is the right atrium which receives deoxygenated blood from the venae cavae.
Final answer: 1 - pulmonary vein; 2 - semilunar (pulmonary) valve; 3 - right atrium / auricle.

hints: First decide which is which in Fig. 5.3. Which chamber, X or Y, has the much thicker muscle wall and which circuit must it supply?
Compare the two circuits - which journey is much longer and has much greater total resistance to flow?
Link muscle thickness to force and pressure. Why is high pressure essential for one circuit but dangerous for the other?
walkthrough:
Matching Thickness to Job**
In Fig. 5.3, Y has a very thick wall and a small round cavity - that is the left ventricle. X has a thinner wall and crescent-shaped cavity - that is the right ventricle. The left ventricle pumps blood around the whole body in the systemic circulation, while the right ventricle only pumps to the nearby lungs in the pulmonary circulation.

Why Systemic Needs More Muscle**
Blood travelling to the brain, gut, legs and back faces a much longer distance and far greater resistance than blood going just to the lungs next door. To overcome that resistance and maintain flow all around the body, high blood pressure is needed. More cardiac muscle in the wall of Y can contract with greater force to generate that high pressure. The thinner right side is enough for low pressure flow, which is important because high pressure would rupture the thin pulmonary capillaries.

Final answer: Chamber Y is left ventricle pumping to systemic circulation, chamber X is right ventricle pumping to pulmonary circulation; systemic route is much longer with greater resistance so higher pressure is needed; thicker muscle in Y generates greater force for high pressure, while lower pressure protects delicate pulmonary capillaries from damage.

hints: Think about where the wave of excitation starts in the heart and which chambers feel it first.
Consider why the atria must finish contracting and empty before the ventricles start, and what stops the impulse spreading straight down.
Recall where the impulse is held up for a fraction of a second and which special fibres then carry it rapidly downwards.
Picture how the impulse spreads up through the ventricle walls to push blood upwards into the arteries.
walkthrough:
Atria First**
Everything starts at the sinoatrial node, the pacemaker in the right atrium wall. It sends out a wave of excitation that spreads across the muscle of both atria. Both atria therefore contract together, atrial systole, pushing blood down into the ventricles. It is vital the ventricles do not contract yet.

A Short Pause Then Ventricles Together**
A layer of fibrous, non-conducting tissue between atria and ventricles stops the wave going straight through. The only route is via the atrioventricular node, where the impulse is delayed for about 0.1 s to let the atria fully empty. The AVN then passes the impulse down the bundle of His and out along Purkyne fibres through the ventricle walls. The ventricles then contract together, ventricular systole, from the apex upwards so blood is squeezed up into the aorta and pulmonary artery.

Final answer: Wave of excitation from SAN spreads across both atria causing atrial systole together before ventricles; fibrous non-conducting tissue blocks direct spread; impulse delayed at AVN then passed via bundle of His to Purkyne fibres in ventricle walls; ventricles contract together from apex upwards to eject blood.
